newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian opposition leader wants French troops out.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian opposition leader wants French troops out.

text.p: Ivory Coast's chief opposition leader Laurent Gbagbo called on Sunday for the departure of French troops based in the West African country.
"Our party is against the idea of the continuous stay on our soil of the French troops based in Port Bouet," Gbagbo told a rally of his Ivorian Popular Front Party (FPI) in Abidjan.

"It's ridiculous that a country like ours that just celebrated its 37 years of independence should still entrust its defence in the hands of a foreign force," Gbagbo said, adding: "We have already prepared a bill that we will introduce in parliament to that effect."
New Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's government plans to cut the number of French troops in Africa by about 40 percent to 5,000 from 8,350, French government sources say.

France established the military bases under defence accords with its former African colonies dating back to their independence in the early 1960s. Opponents in Africa and France say their presence has helped shore up African dictators.

Jospin's government is trying to redefine its relationship with France's African allies in line with the end of Cold War rivalry on the continent. It also cites professional and budgetary reasons for the troops cutbacks.
France last week announced the first bases on its hit list -- the Bouar camp in the north of the Central African Republic and another in the capital Bangui with a combined 1,400 troops.
Political sources in Ivory Coast say the government of President Henri Konan Bedie has urged France to keep its marine infantry battalion based in the Abidjan suburb of Port Bouet.

Gbagbo, whose party successfully campaigned for the end of one party rule in Ivory Coast, also called for a slimmer Ivorian national army. He called for the transfer of some soldiers to the police force to help combat crime.

"We don't need combat ready troops in our country," Gbagbo said. "We want the Ivorian army's size to be cut and those soldiers affected to be switched over to the police and gendarmerie forces to help fight the increasing tide of criminality that has enveloped our nation in recent times."
The opposition leader also lashed out against Bedie's government for taking delivery last week of five South African-built police armoured vehicles.

"It's a shame that, the same armoured cars that were used to fight the ANC (African National Congress) during the aparthied days is what an African country like ours would buy," Gbagbo said, calling on the government to send back the vehicles.

However, Gbagbo commended Bedie for constitutional reform plans that would make the president of a planned senate the automatic interim successor to the head of state in case of death or incapacitation.
Under the draft reform, the interim head of state cannot be a candidate for subsequesnt elections for a new president.

Bedie, as parliamentary speaker at the time, became interim president at the death of veteran head of state Felix Houphouet-Boigny in December 1993. He was elected in his own right for a five-year term in October 1995.
